title: "Disorganised"
topic: Responding to criticism, feedback and your own underperformance
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a general medical ward. On the post-take ward round you present a new patient. Halfway through, your consultant interrupts and says in front of the team, "This is disorganised. I can't follow it. Let's move on."

You feel embarrassed. You had been on call all night and had little time to prepare.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Explain to the consultant in front of the team that you had little time to prepare.
options.brief: Sounds defensive and is unlikely to help in the moment.
options.detailed: Your reason is genuine, but raising it in front of the team, during the ward round, is likely to come across as an excuse and won't help either of you.

options.text: Raise a formal complaint about being criticised in public.
options.brief: Disproportionate for a single comment about a presentation.
options.detailed: Repeated public humiliation can be a form of undermining and may need raising. But a single critical comment about your presentation is better addressed by seeking feedback.

options.text: Ask the registrar to present your patients for the rest of the week.
options.brief: Avoiding the task stops you improving.
options.detailed: This avoids further embarrassment but means you miss the chance to improve, and adds to your registrar's workload.

options.text: Ask the consultant later for specific feedback on how to improve.
options.brief: Turns criticism into something you can act on.
options.detailed: General criticism is hard to learn from. Asking, at a calmer moment, what would have made the presentation easier to follow gives you concrete things to work on and shows you take feedback seriously.

options.text: Accept that the consultant is hard to please, and carry on as before.
options.brief: Dismisses feedback that might be useful.
options.detailed: Some consultants are more critical than others, but writing off the feedback means missing the chance to improve.

options.text: Reflect on the feedback, and use a clear structure for future presentations.
options.detailed: Even if the delivery was harsh, the feedback may be useful. Thinking about what went wrong, and using a consistent structure for presentations, will help you next time.

options.text: Tell your colleagues that the consultant was unfair to you.
options.brief: Doesn't help you improve and may create tension.
options.detailed: It's natural to want sympathy, but complaining to colleagues doesn't address the feedback and may affect team relationships.

options.text: Practise presenting cases with a colleague or your registrar.
options.detailed: Rehearsing with a colleague, or asking your registrar to watch you present, gives you a chance to improve in a supportive setting.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond to critical feedback given publicly: constructively, without defensiveness or overreaction.
explanation.keyDetails: The comment was blunt and public. You were tired after a night on call. The criticism may still be partly fair.
explanation.reasoning: [D], [F] and [H] all use the feedback to improve. The distractors are defensive ([A]), disproportionate ([B]), avoidant ([C], [E]), or unconstructive ([G]).
explanation.competing: [B] would become appropriate if the consultant repeatedly humiliated you or others; a single comment is better addressed directly.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, reflecting on feedback and developing your practice.
